parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the exact length of the arc of the curve y = cosh x from x = 0 to x = ln 3.
parts.working:
M1: s = ∫√(1 + sinh²x) dx = ∫ cosh x dx
A1: [sinh x]₀^(ln 3)
M1: sinh(ln 3) = (3 − 1/3)/2
A1: 4/3

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve is defined parametrically by x = t², y = (2/3)t³, for 0 ≤ t ≤ √3. Show that (dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)² = 4t²(1 + t²).
parts.working:
M1: dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 2t²
A1: 4t² + 4t⁴ = 4t²(1 + t²) (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact length of the curve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A wire is bent into the shape of this curve, with lengths in centimetres. A second wire of the same shape is made from the curve for 0 ≤ t ≤ T. Find T if the second wire is exactly half as long as the first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = x²/2 − (1/4) ln x for x > 0. Show that 1 + (dy/dx)² = (x + 1/(4x))².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact length of the arc of C from x = 1 to x = 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The arc of the curve y = 2√x from x = 0 to x = 3 is rotated through 2π radians about the x-axis. Find the exact area of the surface generated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve is given parametrically by x = cos³t, y = sin³t, for 0 ≤ t ≤ π/2. Show that (dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)² = 9sin²t cos²t.
parts.working:
M1: dx/dt = −3cos²t sin t, dy/dt = 3sin²t cos t
M1: 9cos⁴t sin²t + 9sin⁴t cos²t = 9sin²t cos²t(cos²t + sin²t)
A1: 9sin²t cos²t (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The curve is rotated through 2π radians about the x-axis. Find the exact area of the surface generated.
parts.working:
M1: S = 2π∫ y √(…) dt = 2π∫₀^(π/2) sin³t × 3 sin t cos t dt
A1: 6π∫₀^(π/2) sin⁴t cos t dt
M1: [sin⁵t/5]₀^(π/2)
A1: 6π/5

parts.label: a
parts.text: A lampshade is modelled by rotating the arc of y = cosh x between x = 0 and x = 1 through 2π radians about the x-axis (units are decimetres). Show that the curved surface area is π(1 + (1/2)sinh 2).
parts.working:
M1: √(1 + sinh²x) = cosh x
M1: S = 2π∫₀¹ cosh²x dx
M1: cosh²x = (1 + cosh 2x)/2
A1: π[x + (1/2)sinh 2x]₀¹
A1: π(1 + (1/2)sinh 2) (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find this area correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A light elastic string has natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 24 N. Find the work done in stretching the string from an extension of 0.2 m to an extension of 0.5 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the tension in the string when its extension is 0.5 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle P of mass 0.5 kg rests on a smooth horizontal table. It is attached to one end of a light spring of natural length 1.2 m and modulus of elasticity 30 N; the other end of the spring is fixed to a point O on the table. P is pulled away from O until OP = 1.6 m and released from rest.
Find the elastic potential energy stored in the spring just before P is released.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of P when the spring first reaches its natural length.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.4 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1.5 m and modulus of elasticity 20 N. The other end of the string is attached to a fixed point O. The particle is released from rest at O and falls vertically. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Show that the greatest extension x m of the string satisfies 10x² − 6x − 9 = 0, and find x.
parts.working:
M1: energy: loss of GPE = gain in EPE at the lowest point
A1: 0.4 × 10 × (1.5 + x) = 20x²/(2 × 1.5)
M1: rearrange: 20x²/3 − 4x − 6 = 0
A1: 10x² − 6x − 9 = 0 (AG)
A1: x = (6 + √396)/20 = 1.29

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest speed of the particle during its fall.
parts.working:
B1: greatest speed where tension = weight: 20e/1.5 = 4, e = 0.3 m
M1: ½(0.4)v² = 4(1.8) − 20(0.3)²/3
A1: v² = 33.0, v = 5.74 m s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At an adventure park in Hunza, a bungee jumper of mass 70 kg is attached to a light elastic rope of natural length 20 m and modulus of elasticity 1750 N. The other end of the rope is fixed to a platform. The jumper steps off the platform from rest and falls vertically. Model the jumper as a particle and ignore air resistance. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the distance below the platform of the lowest point reached by the jumper.
parts.working:
M1: let extension at lowest point be x: 700(20 + x) = 1750x²/(2 × 20)
A1: 43.75x² − 700x − 14000 = 0, i.e. x² − 16x − 320 = 0
M1: solve: x = 8 + √384 = 27.6
A1: lowest point 47.6 m below the platform

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest speed of the jumper.
parts.working:
B1: greatest speed at equilibrium: 1750e/20 = 700, e = 8 m
M1: ½(70)v² = 700 × 28 − 1750 × 8²/40
A1: v² = 480, v = 21.9 m s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which the model may be unrealistic.
parts.answer: Air resistance is ignored (or the rope's mass / the jumper's size are ignored).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A block of mass 2 kg lies on a rough horizontal floor, where the coefficient of friction is 0.25. It is attached to one end of a light spring of natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 40 N, the other end of which is fixed to a wall. The block is pulled away from the wall until the extension is 0.3 m, and released from rest. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Show that the block begins to move.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the block when the spring reaches its natural length.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the greatest compression of the spring, and show that the block then remains at rest.
parts.answer: 0.1 m; the thrust (5 N) equals the limiting friction, so the block stays at rest.
parts.working:
M1: 0.75 = 40c²/1.6 + 5c
A1: 25c² + 5c − 0.75 = 0
A1: c = 0.1 m
B1: thrust 40 × 0.1/0.8 = 5 N = F_max, so it does not move back

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.5 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1.2 m and modulus of elasticity 15 N. The other end of the string is fixed to a point A on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The particle is released from rest at A and slides down the line of greatest slope through A. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the distance travelled by the particle before it first comes to instantaneous rest.
parts.working:
M1: energy: mg sin 30° × d = λ(d − 1.2)²/(2 × 1.2)
A1: 2.5d = 6.25(d − 1.2)²
M1: 6.25d² − 17.5d + 9 = 0
A1: d = 2.12 m (the other root is less than 1.2 and is rejected)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the particle when it has travelled 1.2 m.
parts.working:
M1: string not yet taut, v² = 2(g sin30°)(1.2) = 12
A1: v = √12 = 3.46 m s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two points A and B are 3 m apart on a smooth horizontal table. A particle P of mass 0.5 kg is attached to two light elastic strings, each of natural length 1 m and modulus of elasticity 10 N. The other end of one string is attached to A and the other end of the second string to B. M is the mid-point of AB.
P is held at rest on AB at the point 0.4 m from M towards B, and released. Show that both strings remain taut throughout the motion.
parts.answer: P moves between points 0.4 m either side of M, so each string's length is at least 1.1 m > 1 m.
parts.working:
M1: by symmetry of energy, P oscillates between the points 0.4 m either side of M
A1: minimum string length 1.5 − 0.4 = 1.1 m > natural length, so both taut

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of P as it passes through M.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the magnitude of the acceleration of P at the instant it is released.
parts.working:
M1: tensions 10(0.9) = 9 N towards A and 10(0.1) = 1 N towards B; resultant 8 N
A1: a = 8/0.5 = 16 m s⁻²

parts.label: a
parts.text: A toy spring gun fires a ball of mass 0.02 kg horizontally. The spring has natural length 0.2 m and modulus of elasticity 400 N. The spring is compressed by 0.05 m and then released, and the ball leaves the spring when the spring reaches its natural length. Ignoring friction, find the speed of the ball as it leaves the gun.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the compression needed for the ball to leave at 20 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A light spring of natural length 0.5 m and modulus of elasticity 200 N stands vertically with its lower end fixed to the ground. A particle of mass 2 kg is released from rest 0.3 m vertically above the top of the spring, lands on it and stays in contact with it. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the greatest compression of the spring.
parts.working:
M1: GPE lost = EPE gained at lowest point
A1: 20(0.3 + x) = 200x²/(2 × 0.5)
M1: 100x² − 10x − 3 = 0
A1: x = (10 + √1300)/200
A1: 0.230 m

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the particle when the compression is 0.1 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.25 kg hangs in equilibrium at the end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.6 m and modulus of elasticity 12 N, whose upper end is fixed at O. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the extension of the string in the equilibrium position.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The particle is projected vertically downwards from the equilibrium position with speed 2 m s⁻¹. Find the greatest extension of the string in the subsequent motion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A rough plane is inclined at an angle α to the horizontal, where tan α = 3/4. A particle of mass 1 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 2 m and modulus of elasticity 20 N. The other end of the string is fixed to a point O on the plane. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is 0.5. The particle is released from rest at O and moves down the line of greatest slope. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Show that the particle comes to instantaneous rest after travelling a distance d m, where 5d² − 22d + 20 = 0, and find d.
parts.working:
B1: normal reaction 10 cos α = 8 N, friction 0.5 × 8 = 4 N
M1: energy: GPE lost = work against friction + EPE
A1: 10 × 0.6 × d = 4d + 20(d − 2)²/(2 × 2)
M1: 2d = 5(d − 2)²
A1: 5d² − 22d + 20 = 0 (AG)
A1: d = (22 + √84)/10 = 3.12 (root > 2)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine whether the particle remains at rest at this point.
parts.answer: Tension 11.2 N > 6 + 4 = 10 N, so it moves back up the slope.
parts.working:
M1: T = 20(1.12)/2 = 11.2 N compared with 10 sin α + F_max = 6 + 4 = 10 N
A1: T > 10, so it does not remain at rest (moves up the plane)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A light elastic string of natural length 0.5 m and modulus of elasticity 30 N has a tension of 12 N. Find the extension of the string.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the elastic potential energy stored in the string.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the additional work needed to double the extension.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two fixed points A and B are 4 m apart with B vertically below A. A particle P of mass 0.6 kg is attached to two light elastic strings, each of natural length 1.5 m and modulus of elasticity 18 N. One string is attached to A and the other to B. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Show that in equilibrium AP = 2.25 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: P is held at rest at the point 2.75 m below A and released. Explain why the lower string is slack at the start of the motion.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the speed of P as it passes through the equilibrium position.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.8 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus of elasticity 32 N. The other end is attached to a fixed point O. The particle is released from rest at O. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the greatest extension of the string.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest speed of the particle.
parts.working:
B1: equilibrium extension 32e = 8, e = 0.25 m
M1: ½(0.8)v² = 8(1.25) − 32(0.25²)/2
A1: v² = 22.5, v = 4.74 m s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A light spring of natural length 0.5 m and modulus of elasticity 50 N lies on a rough horizontal surface with one end fixed at O. A particle of mass 0.4 kg is attached to the other end. The particle is at the point where the spring has its natural length, moving towards O with speed 3 m s⁻¹. The coefficient of friction is 0.3. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the greatest compression of the spring.
parts.working:
B1: friction = 0.3 × 4 = 1.2 N
M1: KE lost = EPE gained + work against friction
A1: 1.8 = 50c²/1 + 1.2c
M1: 50c² + 1.2c − 1.8 = 0
A1: c = 0.178 m

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine whether the particle stays at rest at the point of greatest compression.
parts.answer: Thrust 17.8 N > 1.2 N, so it moves back.
parts.working:
M1: thrust = 50(0.178)/0.5 = 17.8 N
A1: greater than maximum friction 1.2 N, so it does not stay at rest

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle of mass 0.3 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.9 m and modulus of elasticity 18 N. The other end is fixed at a point O on a smooth horizontal surface. The particle is held at rest with the string of length 1.5 m and then released. Find the speed of the particle when the string becomes slack.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time taken, from the moment the string becomes slack, for the particle to reach O.
parts.working:
M1: string slack: constant speed over 0.9 m
A1: t = 0.9/√24 = 0.184 s

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A light spring of natural length 0.6 m and modulus of elasticity 30 N lies along a line of greatest slope of a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Its lower end is fixed at the bottom of the plane and a particle of mass 0.5 kg is attached to its upper end. The particle is held at rest with the spring compressed to a length of 0.4 m, and then released. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the speed of the particle when the spring reaches its natural length.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest extension of the spring in the subsequent motion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.5 kg hangs in equilibrium from a light elastic string of natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 20 N, whose upper end is fixed at O. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the equilibrium extension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The particle is pulled down until the extension is 0.6 m and released from rest. Find the speed of the particle when the string becomes slack.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance below O of the highest point reached by the particle.
parts.working:
M1: after the string is slack, the particle moves freely under gravity: h = v²/(2g) = 6/20 = 0.3 m
M1: highest point is 0.3 m above the natural-length position, which is 0.8 m below O
A1: 0.5 m below O

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 1.5 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus of elasticity 30 N. The other end is fixed at a point O on a rough horizontal table. The particle is released from rest when the extension is 0.5 m. It first comes to rest when the extension is 0.1 m. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the coefficient of friction between the particle and the table.
parts.working:
M1: EPE lost = 30(0.25 − 0.01)/2 = 3.6 J
M1: work against friction = μ × 15 × 0.4 = 6μ
M1: 6μ = 3.6
A1: μ = 0.6

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the particle remains at rest at this position.
parts.working:
M1: T = 30 × 0.1/1 = 3 N, F_max = 0.6 × 15 = 9 N
A1: 3 < 9, so it remains at rest

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.2 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.5 m. The other end is attached to a fixed point O. The particle is released from rest at O and its lowest point is 1.3 m below O. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the modulus of elasticity of the string.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest speed of the particle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the acceleration of the particle at its lowest point.
parts.working:
M1: tension = λ(0.8)/0.5 = 6.5 N; 6.5 − 2 = 0.2a
A1: a = 22.5 m s⁻² upwards

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.3 kg hangs from a light elastic string of natural length 0.5 m and modulus of elasticity 15 N, whose upper end is fixed. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Show that the extension in equilibrium is 0.1 m.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: The particle is pulled down until the extension is 0.25 m and released from rest. Find its speed as it passes through the equilibrium position.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a warehouse in Karachi, a crate of mass 20 kg is released from rest on a smooth ramp inclined at angle α to the horizontal, where sin α = 0.25. At the bottom of the ramp is a buffer: a light spring of natural length 0.5 m and modulus of elasticity 4000 N lying along the line of greatest slope, with its lower end fixed. The crate starts 2 m up the slope from the free end of the spring. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the greatest compression of the spring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the compression of the spring when the speed of the crate is greatest.
parts.working:
M1: greatest speed when thrust = component of weight: 4000c/0.5 = 50
A1: c = 0.00625 m

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.5 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus of elasticity 10 N. The other end of the string is fixed at a point O on a rough horizontal surface; the coefficient of friction is 0.2. The particle is released from rest with the string stretched along the surface to a length of 1.6 m. The particle can pass over O without obstruction. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the speed of the particle when the string becomes slack.
parts.working:
B1: friction = 0.2 × 5 = 1 N (and tension 6 N > 1 N, so it moves)
M1: EPE = 10(0.6²)/2 = 1.8 J; work against friction = 1 × 0.6
M1: ½(0.5)v² = 1.8 − 0.6
A1: v² = 4.8, v = 2.19 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total distance travelled by the particle before it comes to rest, and state where it comes to rest.
parts.answer: 1.8 m; 0.2 m beyond O (on the opposite side from its starting point)
parts.working:
M1: slack string: deceleration 1/0.5 = 2 m s⁻²
M1: distance = 4.8/(2 × 2) = 1.2 m
B1: 1.2 m < 2 m, so the string does not become taut again on the other side
A1: total 0.6 + 1.2 = 1.8 m; stops 0.2 m past O

parts.label: a
parts.text:
When a particle of mass 0.3 kg hangs in equilibrium from a light spring, the length of the spring is 0.65 m. When the particle is replaced by one of mass 0.5 kg, the length in equilibrium is 0.75 m. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the natural length and the modulus of elasticity of the spring.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 1.2 kg is attached to one end of each of two identical light elastic strings, each of natural length 0.6 m. The other ends of the strings are attached to the points A and B, which are 1.6 m apart on the same horizontal level. In equilibrium the particle is 0.6 m vertically below the mid-point of AB. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the tension in each string.
parts.working:
B1: each string has length √(0.8² + 0.6²) = 1 m; cos θ = 0.6 with the vertical
M1: 2T(0.6) = 12
A1: T = 10 N

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the modulus of elasticity of the strings.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 2 kg rests on a smooth plane inclined at an angle θ to the horizontal, where sin θ = 0.6. It is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 40 N; the other end is fixed to a point higher up the same line of greatest slope. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the extension of the string in equilibrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A horizontal force of magnitude P N, acting in the vertical plane containing the line of greatest slope and towards the plane, is now applied so that the particle rests in equilibrium with the string at its natural length. Find P.
parts.working:
M1: resolve along slope: P cos θ = 20 sin θ
A1: P × 0.8 = 12
A1: P = 15

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A uniform rod AB of mass 3 kg and length 1.2 m is freely hinged at A to a vertical wall. It is held horizontally in equilibrium by a light elastic string of natural length 1.2 m joining B to the point C on the wall 0.9 m vertically above A. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the tension in the string.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the modulus of elasticity of the string.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the magnitude of the force exerted by the hinge on the rod.
parts.working:
M1: horizontal: H = 25 × 0.8 = 20 N
M1: vertical: V = 30 − 25 × 0.6 = 15 N
A1: √(20² + 15²) = 25 N

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two fixed points A and B are 2 m apart, with A vertically above B. A particle P of mass 0.5 kg is attached to A by a light spring of natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 20 N, and to B by a light spring of natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 30 N. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the length AP when P is in equilibrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the lower spring is stretched or compressed in this position.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 4 kg is on a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal, where the coefficient of friction is 0.2. It is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus of elasticity 50 N; the other end of the string is fixed at a point O higher up the same line of greatest slope. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the least and greatest possible distances of the particle from O when it is in equilibrium. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.working:
B1: R = 40 cos 30° = 34.64 N, F_max = 0.2R = 6.928 N
M1: least extension when friction acts up the slope: T + F = 40 sin 30°
A1: T = 13.07 N, x = T/50 = 0.261 m, distance 1.26 m
M1: greatest when friction acts down the slope: T = 20 + F
A1: T = 26.93 N, x = 0.539 m
A1: distance 1.54 m

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.6 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.5 m and modulus of elasticity 12 N. The other end of the string is fixed at O. The particle is held in equilibrium by a horizontal force of magnitude P N, with the string inclined at angle θ to the downward vertical, where tan θ = 3/4. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find P and the tension in the string.
parts.working:
M1: resolve vertically: T cos θ = 6, T = 6/0.8
A1: T = 7.5 N
A1: P = T sin θ = 4.5

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the depth of the particle below O.
parts.working:
M1: extension = 7.5 × 0.5/12 = 0.3125 m
M1: length 0.8125 m; depth = 0.8125 cos θ
A1: 0.65 m

parts.label: c
parts.text: The force is changed so that, in a new equilibrium, the string is inclined at 60° to the downward vertical, with the horizontal force still acting. Find the new length of the string.
parts.working:
M1: T cos 60° = 6, T = 12 N
A1: extension = 12 × 0.5/12 = 0.5 m, length 1 m

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The lifetimes of AA batteries of brand A are normally distributed with standard deviation 4.2 hours, and those of brand B are normally distributed with standard deviation 3.8 hours. A random sample of 30 brand A batteries has mean lifetime 52.3 hours, and a random sample of 25 brand B batteries has mean lifetime 50.1 hours.
Test, at the 5% significance level, whether the mean lifetime of brand A batteries is greater than that of brand B batteries.
parts.answer: z = 2.038 > 1.645: reject H₀; there is sufficient evidence that brand A batteries last longer on average.
parts.working:
B1: H₀: μ_A = μ_B, H₁: μ_A > μ_B
M1: standard error √(4.2²/30 + 3.8²/25) = 1.080
A1: z = 2.2/1.080 = 2.038
B1: critical value 1.645
M1: compare: 2.038 > 1.645, reject H₀
A1: sufficient evidence at 5% that brand A has a greater mean lifetime

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An agricultural researcher in Punjab measures the heights, x cm, of wheat plants grown with two fertilisers, P and Q. Summary results are:
Fertiliser P: n = 50, Σx = 1285, Σx² = 33410.5
Fertiliser Q: n = 60, Σx = 1497, Σx² = 37720.8
Find unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance for each fertiliser.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test, at the 5% significance level, whether there is a difference between the mean heights for the two fertilisers.
parts.answer: z = 1.465; |z| < 1.96, so do not reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence of a difference in mean heights.
parts.working:
B1: H₀: μ_P = μ_Q, H₁: μ_P ≠ μ_Q
M1: z = (25.7 − 24.95)/√(7.878/50 + 6.282/60)
A1: z = 1.465
B1: critical values ±1.96
A1: do not reject H₀; insufficient evidence of a difference

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it was not necessary to assume that the heights are normally distributed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Σ (from r = 1 to n) r(r + 2) = (1/6)n(n + 1)(2n + 7).
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: LHS = 1 × 3 = 3, RHS = (1/6)(1)(2)(9) = 3.
M1: assume true for n = k and add the (k + 1)th term (k + 1)(k + 3).
M1: factorise (1/6)(k + 1)[k(2k + 7) + 6(k + 3)] = (1/6)(k + 1)(2k² + 13k + 18).
A1: = (1/6)(k + 1)(k + 2)(2k + 9) = (1/6)(k + 1)((k + 1) + 1)(2(k + 1) + 7).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Σ (from r = 1 to n) 1/((2r − 1)(2r + 1)) = n/(2n + 1).
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: LHS = 1/(1 × 3) = 1/3, RHS = 1/3.
M1: assume true for n = k; add 1/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)).
M1: common denominator: [k(2k + 3) + 1]/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)) = (2k² + 3k + 1)/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)).
A1: = (k + 1)(2k + 1)/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)) = (k + 1)/(2(k + 1) + 1).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.text: The sequence u₁, u₂, u₃, … is defined by u₁ = 3 and u_(n+1) = 2u_n − 1 for n ≥ 1. Find u₅.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that u_n = 2ⁿ + 1 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 2¹ + 1 = 3 = u₁.
M1: assume u_k = 2ᵏ + 1; then u_(k+1) = 2(2ᵏ + 1) − 1.
A1: = 2^(k+1) + 1.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Σ (from r = 1 to n) r × r! = (n + 1)! − 1.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: LHS = 1 × 1! = 1, RHS = 2! − 1 = 1.
M1: assume true for n = k; add (k + 1)(k + 1)!.
M1: (k + 1)! − 1 + (k + 1)(k + 1)! = (k + 1)!(1 + k + 1) − 1.
A1: = (k + 2)(k + 1)! − 1 = (k + 2)! − 1.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 2 × 3⁰ − 1 = 1 = u₁.
M1: assume u_k = 2 × 3^(k−1) − 1; u_(k+1) = 3(2 × 3^(k−1) − 1) + 2.
A1: = 2 × 3ᵏ − 3 + 2 = 2 × 3ᵏ − 1.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a

Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Σ (from r = 1 to n) r × 2ʳ = (n − 1)2^(n+1) + 2.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: LHS = 2, RHS = 0 + 2 = 2.
M1: assume true for n = k; add (k + 1)2^(k+1).
M1: (k − 1)2^(k+1) + (k + 1)2^(k+1) + 2 = 2k × 2^(k+1) + 2.
A1: = k × 2^(k+2) + 2 = ((k + 1) − 1)2^((k+1)+1) + 2.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that 2ⁿ > n² for all integers n ≥ 5.
parts.working:
B1: n = 5: 2⁵ = 32 > 25.
M1: assume 2ᵏ > k² for some k ≥ 5; then 2^(k+1) = 2 × 2ᵏ > 2k².
M1: 2k² − (k + 1)² = k² − 2k − 1 = (k − 1)² − 2 > 0 for k ≥ 5 (indeed for k ≥ 3).
A1: so 2^(k+1) > (k + 1)².
A1: true for n = 5 and true for k + 1 whenever true for k ≥ 5, so true for all n ≥ 5.

M1: = [2/(2k − 1)] ÷ [(2k + 1)/(2k − 1)].
A1: = 2/(2k + 1) = 2/(2(k + 1) − 1).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that 3ⁿ ≥ 2n² + 1 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 3 ≥ 3 true.
M1: assume 3ᵏ ≥ 2k² + 1; then 3^(k+1) ≥ 3(2k² + 1) = 6k² + 3.
M1: compare with 2(k + 1)² + 1 = 2k² + 4k + 3.
M1: (6k² + 3) − (2k² + 4k + 3) = 4k² − 4k = 4k(k − 1) ≥ 0 for k ≥ 1.
A1: so 3^(k+1) ≥ 2(k + 1)² + 1.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 0 < 1 < 3.
M1: assume 0 < u_k < 3; then 6 < u_k + 6 < 9.
A1: so √6 < u_(k+1) < 3, hence 0 < u_(k+1) < 3.
A1: conclusion for all n.

parts.working:
M1: u_(n+1)² − u_n² = u_n + 6 − u_n² = −(u_n − 3)(u_n + 2).
A1: since 0 < u_n < 3, (u_n − 3) < 0 and (u_n + 2) > 0, so u_(n+1)² > u_n².
A1: both terms positive, so u_(n+1) > u_n.

parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 3 − 2 = 1; n = 2: 9 − 4 = 5 (both base cases needed).
M1: assume u_k = 3ᵏ − 2ᵏ and u_(k+1) = 3^(k+1) − 2^(k+1).
M1: u_(k+2) = 5(3^(k+1) − 2^(k+1)) − 6(3ᵏ − 2ᵏ).
M1: = 3ᵏ(15 − 6) − 2ᵏ(10 − 6) = 9 × 3ᵏ − 4 × 2ᵏ.
A1: = 3^(k+2) − 2^(k+2).
A1: true for n = 1, 2 and if true for n = k and k + 1 then true for k + 2, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 1 ≤ 2 − 1 = 1.
M1: assume Σ (1 to k) 1/r² ≤ 2 − 1/k; then Σ (1 to k + 1) ≤ 2 − 1/k + 1/(k + 1)².
M1: need −1/k + 1/(k + 1)² ≤ −1/(k + 1), i.e. 1/(k + 1)² ≤ 1/k − 1/(k + 1) = 1/(k(k + 1)).
A1: true since k(k + 1) < (k + 1)².
A1: so Σ (1 to k + 1) 1/r² ≤ 2 − 1/(k + 1).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that y = x eˣ, prove by mathematical induction that dⁿy/dxⁿ = (x + n)eˣ for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: dy/dx = eˣ + x eˣ = (x + 1)eˣ.
M1: assume dᵏy/dxᵏ = (x + k)eˣ; differentiate using the product rule.
A1: d^(k+1)y/dx^(k+1) = eˣ + (x + k)eˣ = (x + k + 1)eˣ.
A1: form (x + (k + 1))eˣ clearly stated.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

B1: n = 1: f′(x) = −2(2x + 1)⁻² = (−2)¹ 1!/(2x + 1)².
M1: assume f⁽ᵏ⁾(x) = (−2)ᵏ k!(2x + 1)^(−(k+1)); differentiate.
A1: f⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾(x) = (−2)ᵏ k! × (−(k + 1)) × 2 × (2x + 1)^(−(k+2)).
A1: = (−2)^(k+1)(k + 1)!/(2x + 1)^(k+2).

B1: n = 1: dy/dx = 1/(1 + x) = (−1)⁰ 0!/(1 + x)¹.
M1: assume dᵏy/dxᵏ = (−1)^(k−1)(k − 1)!(1 + x)^(−k); differentiate.
A1: = (−1)^(k−1)(k − 1)! × (−k)(1 + x)^(−k−1).
A1: = (−1)ᵏ k!/(1 + x)^(k+1).

A1: d^(k+1)y/dx^(k+1) = 3^(k+1) cos(3x + kπ/2).
A1: = 3^(k+1) sin(3x + kπ/2 + π/2) = 3^(k+1) sin(3x + (k + 1)π/2).

parts.text:
Given that y = x² e^(2x), prove by mathematical induction that
dⁿy/dxⁿ = 2^(n−2) e^(2x) (4x² + 4nx + n(n − 1)) for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: dy/dx = 2x e^(2x) + 2x² e^(2x) = 2⁻¹ e^(2x)(4x² + 4x) ✓.
M1: assume true for n = k; differentiate the product.
M1: d/dx[2^(k−2) e^(2x)(4x² + 4kx + k(k − 1))] = 2^(k−2) e^(2x)[2(4x² + 4kx + k² − k) + 8x + 4k].
A1: = 2^(k−1) e^(2x)[4x² + 4(k + 1)x + k² + k].
A1: k² + k = (k + 1)k, giving the formula with n = k + 1.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that y = eˣ cos x, prove by mathematical induction that dⁿy/dxⁿ = 2^(n/2) eˣ cos(x + nπ/4) for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: dy/dx = eˣ(cos x − sin x) = √2 eˣ cos(x + π/4).
M1: assume dᵏy/dxᵏ = 2^(k/2) eˣ cos(x + kπ/4); differentiate.
A1: = 2^(k/2) eˣ[cos(x + kπ/4) − sin(x + kπ/4)].
M1: use cos A − sin A = √2 cos(A + π/4).
A1: = 2^((k+1)/2) eˣ cos(x + (k + 1)π/4).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.working:

B1: n = 2: d²y/dx² = 1/x = (−1)² 0!/x¹.
M1: assume dᵏy/dxᵏ = (−1)ᵏ (k − 2)! x^(−(k−1)); differentiate.
A1: = (−1)ᵏ (k − 2)! × (−(k − 1)) x^(−k).
A1: = (−1)^(k+1) (k − 1)!/xᵏ, the formula with n = k + 1.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Remainder 8; n = 2 is a counter-example (88 is not a multiple of 16).
parts.working:

A1: remainder 8 ≠ 0, so one counter-example disproves the statement; a true base case alone proves nothing.

M1: = 2(2^(k+2) + 3^(2k+1)) + 7 × 3^(2k+1).
A1: = 14m + 7 × 3^(2k+1) = 7(2m + 3^(2k+1)).

parts.working:
B1: n = 1: (6 − 2, 3 − 6; 4 − 2, 3 − 4) = (4 −3; 2 −1) = M.
M1: assume formula for Mᵏ; form M^(k+1) = Mᵏ M.
M1: top-left: 4(3 × 2ᵏ − 2) + 2(3 − 3 × 2ᵏ) = 6 × 2ᵏ − 2 = 3 × 2^(k+1) − 2; top-right: −3(3 × 2ᵏ − 2) − (3 − 3 × 2ᵏ) = 3 − 6 × 2ᵏ = 3 − 3 × 2^(k+1).
A1: bottom-left: 4(2^(k+1) − 2) + 2(3 − 2^(k+1)) = 2^(k+2) − 2.
A1: bottom-right: −3(2^(k+1) − 2) − (3 − 2^(k+1)) = 3 − 2^(k+2).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

M1: e^(2y) − 2x e^y + 1 = 0.

A1: y ≥ 0 needs e^y ≥ 1; the product of the roots is 1, so the larger root x + √(x² − 1) is taken.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of arcosh(5/3) + arcosh(17/8), simplifying your answer to a single logarithm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove that artanh x = (1/2) ln((1 + x)/(1 − x)) for −1 < x < 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express artanh(1/3) + artanh(1/5) as a single logarithm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using exponentials, prove that sinh 3x = 3 sinh x + 4 sinh³x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that sinh x = 1/2, find the exact value of sinh 3x.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the definitions sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2 and cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2. Prove that cosh(x + y) = cosh x cosh y + sinh x sinh y.
parts.working:
M1: cosh x cosh y = (e^(x+y) + e^(x−y) + e^(−x+y) + e^(−x−y))/4.
M1: sinh x sinh y = (e^(x+y) − e^(x−y) − e^(−x+y) + e^(−x−y))/4.
M1: add: (2e^(x+y) + 2e^(−x−y))/4.
A1: = cosh(x + y).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that sinh a = 3/4 and sinh b = 5/12, with a, b > 0, find the exact value of cosh(a + b).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove that 1 − tanh²x = sech²x.
parts.working:
M1: divide cosh²x − sinh²x = 1 by cosh²x.
A1: 1 − tanh²x = sech²x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that tanh x = −5/13, find the exact values of cosh x and sinh x.
parts.working:
M1: sech²x = 1 − 25/169 = 144/169.
A1: cosh x = 13/12 (cosh x ≥ 1).
A1: sinh x = tanh x cosh x = −5/12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that x = ln(2 + √3), find the exact values of cosh x, sinh x and tanh x.
parts.answer: cosh x = 2, sinh x = √3, tanh x = √3/2

check: abs(math.cosh(math.log(2+math.sqrt(3))) - 2) < 1e-12 and abs(math.sinh(math.log(2+math.sqrt(3))) - math.sqrt(3)) < 1e-12 and abs(math.tanh(math.log(2+math.sqrt(3))) - math.sqrt(3)/2) < 1e-12
author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that cosh 2t = (1 + tanh²t)/(1 − tanh²t).
parts.working:
M1: cosh 2t = cosh²t + sinh²t.
M1: divide numerator and denominator by cosh²t, using cosh²t − sinh²t = 1.
A1: = (1 + tanh²t)/(1 − tanh²t).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of cosh(2 artanh(1/2)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using exponentials, prove that cosh 3x = 4cosh³x − 3 cosh x.
parts.working:
M1: 4cosh³x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)³/2 = (e^(3x) + 3eˣ + 3e⁻ˣ + e^(−3x))/2.
M1: 3 cosh x = (3eˣ + 3e⁻ˣ)/2.
M1: subtract.
A1: = (e^(3x) + e^(−3x))/2 = cosh 3x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that cosh x = 5/4, find the exact value of cosh 3x, and verify your answer by first finding x as a logarithm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the result for tanh(x + y) in terms of tanh x and tanh y, which you should first prove from the addition formulae for sinh and cosh, show that tanh 2x = 2 tanh x/(1 + tanh²x).
parts.working:
M1: tanh(x + y) = (sinh x cosh y + cosh x sinh y)/(cosh x cosh y + sinh x sinh y).
M1: divide top and bottom by cosh x cosh y.
A1: = (tanh x + tanh y)/(1 + tanh x tanh y).
A1: put y = x: tanh 2x = 2 tanh x/(1 + tanh²x).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that tanh 2x = 4/5, find the exact value of tanh x.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 5 cosh x + 3 sinh x in the form R cosh(x + α), where R > 0, giving R exactly and α as a logarithm.
parts.working:
M1: R cosh x cosh α + R sinh x sinh α: R cosh α = 5, R sinh α = 3.
A1: R² = 25 − 9 = 16, R = 4.
M1: tanh α = 3/5 ⇒ α = (1/2) ln((1 + 3/5)/(1 − 3/5)).
A1: α = (1/2) ln 4 = ln 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the minimum value of 5 cosh x + 3 sinh x and the value of x at which it occurs.
parts.working:
B1: minimum of cosh is 1 when x + ln 2 = 0.
B1: value 4 at x = −ln 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove that sinh x + sinh y = 2 sinh((x + y)/2) cosh((x − y)/2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence show that sinh 3x + sinh x = 0 has only one real solution.
parts.working:
M1: 2 sinh 2x cosh x = 0; cosh x ≥ 1 never zero.
A1: sinh 2x = 0 ⇒ x = 0 only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By writing each side in logarithmic form, show that artanh x = arsinh(x/√(1 − x²)) for −1 < x < 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use this result to find the exact value of x for which artanh x = arsinh(1).
parts.working:
M1: x/√(1 − x²) = 1 ⇒ x² = 1 − x².
A1: x = 1/√2 (positive since arsinh 1 > 0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that cosh 2y = 2cosh²y − 1 and hence prove that arcosh(2x² − 1) = 2 arcosh x for x ≥ 1.
parts.working:
B1: cosh 2y = 2cosh²y − 1 (from exponentials or cosh 2y = cosh²y + sinh²y).
M1: let y = arcosh x ≥ 0, so cosh y = x.
M1: cosh 2y = 2x² − 1, and 2y ≥ 0.
A1: so 2y = arcosh(2x² − 1), i.e. arcosh(2x² − 1) = 2 arcosh x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of arcosh 7 in terms of a single logarithm of a number of the form a + b√3, where a and b are integers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that sinh x = −2, find the exact values of cosh x and tanh x.
parts.working:
M1: cosh²x = 1 + 4 = 5, cosh x > 0.
A1: cosh x = √5, tanh x = −2/√5 = −2√5/5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of x, and show that sinh 2x + cosh 2x = 9 − 4√5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 3 cosh x − sinh x = 3, giving your answers in exact form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 2 cosh x = 5, giving your answers as logarithms in exact form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the positive solution correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation cosh 2x − 5 sinh x = 4, giving your answers as logarithms in exact form.
parts.working:
M1: use cosh 2x = 1 + 2sinh²x.
M1: 2sinh²x − 5 sinh x − 3 = 0.
A1: (2 sinh x + 1)(sinh x − 3) = 0, sinh x = 3 or −1/2.
A1: x = ln(3 + √10).
A1: x = ln(−1/2 + √(5/4)) = ln((√5 − 1)/2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 2 cosh 2x − 9 cosh x + 7 = 0, giving your answers in exact logarithmic form where appropriate.
parts.working:
M1: cosh 2x = 2cosh²x − 1.
M1: 4cosh²x − 9 cosh x + 5 = 0.
A1: (cosh x − 1)(4 cosh x − 5) = 0.
A1: cosh x = 1 ⇒ x = 0.
A1: cosh x = 5/4 ⇒ x = ±ln 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 3 sech²x + 4 tanh x + 1 = 0, giving your answer in the form a ln b.
parts.working:
M1: sech²x = 1 − tanh²x.
M1: 3tanh²x − 4 tanh x − 4 = 0.
A1: (3 tanh x + 2)(tanh x − 2) = 0.
A1: tanh x = 2 rejected (|tanh x| < 1); tanh x = −2/3.
A1: x = (1/2) ln((1/3)/(5/3)) = −(1/2) ln 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 13 cosh x − 5 sinh x in the form R cosh(x − α), where R > 0 and α is given as a logarithm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve 13 cosh x − 5 sinh x = 13.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that sinh 3x = 3 sinh x + 4 sinh³x, solve the equation sinh 3x = 7 sinh x, giving the non-zero solutions as logarithms in exact form.
parts.working:
M1: 4sinh³x − 4 sinh x = 0.
M1: 4 sinh x (sinh x − 1)(sinh x + 1) = 0.
A1: sinh x = 0 ⇒ x = 0.
A1: sinh x = 1 ⇒ x = ln(1 + √2).
A1: sinh x = −1 ⇒ x = ln(√2 − 1) = −ln(1 + √2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the equation tanh x + sech x = 7/5 can be written as e^(2x) − 5eˣ + 6 = 0.
parts.working:
M1: multiply by cosh x: sinh x + 1 = (7/5) cosh x.
M1: (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2 + 1 = (7/10)(eˣ + e⁻ˣ); multiply by 10eˣ.
M1: 5e^(2x) − 5 + 10eˣ = 7e^(2x) + 7.
A1: 2e^(2x) − 10eˣ + 12 = 0 ⇒ e^(2x) − 5eˣ + 6 = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve tanh x + sech x = 7/5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle of mass 0.3 kg is attached to one end of a light inextensible string of length 0.8 m. The other end is fixed to a point O on a smooth horizontal table. The particle moves on the table in a horizontal circle with centre O at a constant speed of 4 m s⁻¹. Find the tension in the string.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the angular speed of the particle and the time it takes to complete one revolution, giving the time correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A conical pendulum consists of a small bob of mass 0.2 kg on a light inextensible string of length 1.25 m, whose upper end is fixed at a point A. The bob moves in a horizontal circle below A with the string inclined at angle θ to the vertical, where cos θ = 0.8. Find the tension in the string.
parts.working:
M1: resolve vertically: T cos θ = mg.
A1: T = 2/0.8 = 2.5 N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the angular speed of the bob.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A car is driven round a horizontal roundabout in Lahore on a circular path of radius 40 m. The coefficient of friction between the tyres and the road is 0.6. Find the greatest speed at which the car can travel without slipping, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working:
M1: friction provides the centripetal force: F = mv²/r.
M1: F ≤ μR = 0.6mg.
A1: v² ≤ 0.6 × 10 × 40 = 240, v ≤ 15.5 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether the answer to part (a) depends on the mass of the car.
parts.answer: No: m cancels from mv²/r ≤ μmg.
parts.working: B1: mass cancels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A horizontal turntable rotates about a vertical axis through its centre O. A small coin rests on the turntable at a distance 0.15 m from O. The coefficient of friction between the coin and the turntable is 0.4. Find the greatest angular speed for which the coin does not slip, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express this angular speed in revolutions per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A section of a motorway near Islamabad is a horizontal circular arc of radius 120 m, banked at 15° to the horizontal. Find the speed at which a car can travel round the bend with no tendency to slip sideways, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working:
M1: vertically R cos 15° = mg.
M1: horizontally R sin 15° = mv²/120.
M1: v² = 120g tan 15°.
A1: v = 17.9 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car travels round the bend faster than this speed. State the direction of the frictional force on the car.
parts.answer: Down the slope of the banking
parts.working: B1: friction acts down the slope to supply extra centripetal force.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle P of mass m moves on the smooth inner surface of a fixed hemispherical bowl of radius a, whose rim is horizontal. P describes a horizontal circle at a depth (3/5)a below the level of the rim, with constant angular speed ω. Show that the normal reaction on P has magnitude (5/3)mg.
parts.working:
M1: the reaction acts along the radius to the centre O of the bowl; its vertical component is R × (3a/5)/a.
M1: R × 3/5 = mg.
A1: R = 5mg/3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find ω in terms of g and a.
parts.working:
B1: radius of circle = √(a² − 9a²/25) = 4a/5.
M1: horizontal component R × (4/5) = mω²(4a/5).
A1: ω² = R/(ma) = 5g/(3a).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A small block A of mass 0.25 kg moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m on a smooth horizontal table. It is attached to a light inextensible string which passes through a small smooth hole O at the centre of the circle. A particle B of mass 0.4 kg hangs at rest at the other end of the string, below the table. Find the speed of A.
parts.working:
M1: T = 0.4g = 4 N (B in equilibrium).
M1: 4 = 0.25v²/0.5.
A1: v² = 8, v = 2.83 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the time taken for A to complete one revolution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². An aircraft of mass 1200 kg flies at a constant speed of 60 m s⁻¹ in a horizontal circle. The lift force acts perpendicular to the wings, which are banked at 30° to the horizontal. Treating the aircraft as a particle, find the magnitude of the lift force, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the radius of the circle, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². In a fairground 'rotor' ride, a person stands against the inside wall of a vertical cylinder of radius 2.5 m, which rotates about its vertical axis. The floor is then lowered. The coefficient of friction between the person and the wall is 0.5. Treating the person as a particle, show that the least angular speed of the cylinder for which the person does not slide down is 2√2 rad s⁻¹.
parts.working:
M1: normal reaction R = mω²r provides centripetal force.
M1: friction balances weight: F = mg with F ≤ μR.
M1: mg ≤ 0.5 × mω² × 2.5.
A1: ω² ≥ 8, ω ≥ 2√2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the person when the cylinder rotates at this least angular speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A bend on a race track is a horizontal circle of radius 50 m, and the track is banked at 20° to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between a car's tyres and the track is 0.3. Find the greatest speed at which the car can go round the bend without slipping up the slope, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working:
M1: friction F = 0.3R acts down the slope at the limiting case.
M1: vertically: R cos 20° − 0.3R sin 20° = mg.
M1: horizontally: R sin 20° + 0.3R cos 20° = mv²/50.
M1: divide: v² = 50g (sin 20° + 0.3 cos 20°)/(cos 20° − 0.3 sin 20°).
A1: v² = 372.7.
A1: v = 19.3 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle P of mass 0.4 kg is attached to two light inextensible strings, each of length 0.5 m. The other ends of the strings are attached to fixed points A and B, where A is 0.8 m vertically above B. P moves in a horizontal circle with both strings taut and with angular speed 6 rad s⁻¹. Find the tension in each string.
parts.working:
B1: P is 0.4 m below A; radius = 0.3 m; each string makes angle θ with the vertical where cos θ = 0.8, sin θ = 0.6.
M1: vertically: 0.8T_A − 0.8T_B = 0.4g ⇒ T_A − T_B = 5.
M1: horizontally: 0.6(T_A + T_B) = 0.4 × 36 × 0.3 = 4.32 ⇒ T_A + T_B = 7.2.
A1: T_A = 6.1 N.
A1: T_B = 1.1 N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the least angular speed for which the string BP is taut.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle of mass 0.4 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.5 m and modulus of elasticity 20 N. The other end of the string is attached to a fixed point O. The particle moves in a horizontal circle below O with the string inclined at angle θ to the vertical, where cos θ = 0.8. Find the extension of the string.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the angular speed of the particle, giving your answer in exact form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A circular test track has radius 80 m and is banked at 25° to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between a vehicle's tyres and the track is 0.2. Find, correct to 3 significant figures, the least speed at which the vehicle can move round the track in a horizontal circle without slipping down the slope.
parts.working:
M1: least speed: friction 0.2R acts up the slope.
M1: R cos 25° + 0.2R sin 25° = mg.
M1: R sin 25° − 0.2R cos 25° = mv²/80.
A1: v² = 80g (sin 25° − 0.2 cos 25°)/(cos 25° + 0.2 sin 25°) = 194.9, v = 14.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest speed at which the vehicle can move round the track without slipping up the slope.
parts.working:
M1: friction acts down the slope: R cos 25° − 0.2R sin 25° = mg; R sin 25° + 0.2R cos 25° = mv²/80.
A1: v² = 587.9.
A1: v = 24.2 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle P of mass m is attached to one end of a light inextensible string of length a, whose other end is fixed at O. P hangs at rest and is then projected horizontally with speed u. Show that P completes vertical circles provided u² ≥ 5ga.
parts.working:
M1: energy: v² at the top = u² − 4ga.
M1: at the top: T + mg = mv²/a.
M1: T ≥ 0 ⇒ v² ≥ ga.
A1: u² − 4ga ≥ ga ⇒ u² ≥ 5ga.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². Find the least value of u when a = 0.9 m, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle is fixed to one end of a light rigid rod of length 0.5 m, freely pivoted at its other end O so that the particle moves in a vertical circle. Find the least speed the particle must have at its lowest point to make complete circles.
parts.working:
M1: a rod can push, so the particle only needs speed ≥ 0 at the top.
M1: u² − 2g(2 × 0.5) ≥ 0.
A1: u ≥ √20 = 4.47 m s⁻¹.
(Strictly u > √20 so that the particle passes over the top; accept u ≥ √20 as the least value.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rod is replaced by a light inextensible string of the same length. Find the new least speed, and explain why it is greater.
parts.answer: 5 m s⁻¹; a string cannot push, so tension ≥ 0 at the top needs v² ≥ ga there.
parts.working:
B1: u² = 5ga = 25, u = 5 m s⁻¹.
B1: explanation: string can only pull.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A small ball moves in a vertical circle on the smooth inner surface of a fixed hollow cylinder of radius 1.6 m, whose axis is horizontal. Its speed at the lowest point is 7 m s⁻¹. Show that the ball does not reach the highest point while in contact with the surface.
parts.working:
M1: needs u² ≥ 5ga = 80 to stay in contact at the top.
A1: 49 < 80, so it leaves the surface first.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the height above the lowest point at which the ball leaves the surface, and its speed at that instant.
parts.answer: Height 2.17 m (exactly 13/6 m); speed 2.38 m s⁻¹
parts.working:
M1: at angle θ from the downward vertical, v² = 49 − 2g(1.6)(1 − cos θ).
M1: R = 0: −mg cos θ = mv²/1.6 (θ > 90°).
A1: cos θ = (32 − 49)/48 = −17/48; height = 1.6(1 + 17/48) = 2.17 m.
A1: v² = −16 cos θ = 17/3, v = 2.38 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle is placed at the highest point of the smooth outer surface of a fixed sphere of radius 0.6 m and given a horizontal speed of √3 m s⁻¹. The particle moves in a vertical plane through the centre. Find, in degrees to 1 decimal place, the angle between the radius to the particle and the upward vertical when the particle leaves the surface.
parts.working:
M1: energy: v² = 3 + 2g(0.6)(1 − cos θ).
M1: radial: mg cos θ − R = mv²/0.6; R = 0.
M1: 6 cos θ = 3 + 12 − 12 cos θ.
A1: cos θ = 15/18 = 5/6.
A1: θ = 33.6°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the speed of the particle at the instant it leaves the surface.
parts.working: B1: v² = 6 cos θ = 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle P of mass m on a light inextensible string of length a is hanging at rest from a fixed point O. It is projected horizontally with speed √(4ga). Show that the string becomes slack when OP makes an angle θ with the downward vertical, where cos θ = −2/3.
parts.working:
M1: energy: v² = 4ga − 2ga(1 − cos θ).
M1: T − mg cos θ = mv²/a.
M1: T = 0: −ga cos θ = 2ga + 2ga cos θ.
A1: cos θ = −2/3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find, in terms of a and g, the height of P above its starting point and its speed at that instant.
parts.working:
B1: height = a(1 − cos θ) = 5a/3.
B1: v² = −ga cos θ = 2ga/3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A particle is projected horizontally with speed u from the highest point of the smooth outer surface of a fixed sphere of radius 2.5 m. Find the set of values of u for which the particle leaves the surface immediately.
parts.working:
M1: at the top, R = mg − mu²/2.5 ≤ 0.
A1: u² ≥ 25, u ≥ 5 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given instead that u = 3 m s⁻¹, find the angle the radius to the particle makes with the upward vertical when it leaves the surface, giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Take g = 10 m s⁻². A smooth solid hemisphere of radius 0.9 m is fixed with its plane face on horizontal ground. A particle is released from rest at the highest point and slides down the curved surface. Show that it leaves the surface when the radius to it makes an angle θ with the upward vertical where cos θ = 2/3, and find its speed then.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance from the centre of the plane face to the point where the particle first hits the ground, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working:
B1: it leaves at height 0.6 m, horizontal distance 0.9 sin θ = 0.6708 m from the centre, with velocity at angle θ below the horizontal.
M1: vertical: 0.6 = (√6 sin θ)t + 5t² ⇒ t = 0.2090 s.
M1: horizontal distance travelled = √6 cos θ × t = 0.3413 m.
A1: total = 1.01 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle P of mass m hangs at rest on a light inextensible string of length a attached to a fixed point O. P is projected horizontally with speed u and the string becomes slack when OP makes an angle of 150° with the downward vertical (that is, OP is 60° above the horizontal). Show that u² = ga(2 + (3/2)√3).
parts.working:
M1: T − mg cos θ = mv²/a with T = 0, θ = 150°: v² = −ga cos 150° = (√3/2)ga.
M1: energy: u² = v² + 2ga(1 − cos 150°).
M1: = (√3/2)ga + 2ga + √3 ga.
A1: = ga(2 + 3√3/2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find, in terms of a, the greatest height above the lowest point reached by P in its subsequent motion.
parts.working:
B1: slack point is a(1 − cos 150°) = a(1 + √3/2) above the lowest point.
M1: velocity is perpendicular to OP, at 30° above the horizontal; vertical component v/2.
M1: further rise = (v/2)²/(2g) = (√3/2)ga/(8g) = √3a/16.
A1: greatest height = a(1 + √3/2 + √3/16) = a(1 + 9√3/16).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle moves on the smooth inner surface of a fixed hollow sphere of radius a, in a vertical great circle. It is projected from the lowest point with speed u and leaves the surface at a height of (3/2)a above the lowest point. Show that u² = (7/2)ga.
parts.working:
M1: height 3a/2 ⇒ the radius makes 60° with the upward vertical (cos θ = −1/2 from the downward vertical).
M1: R = 0: v² = ga/2.
